title: Jonah and the Smile
premise: Urban explorer Mara Vasquez discovers a tunnel network beneath her city that appears on no survey, and in its walls she finds photographs of her grandmother's house — every one showing an extra chair that shouldn't exist. The chair belongs to the Smiling Man, a figure sustained by a song sung in the tunnels, who feeds on those who belong to him and erases everyone who remembers them. When Mara's brother Jonah is pulled into the tunnels mid-photograph, she must learn the song's forbidden last verse from the tunnel's first victim without ever singing along herself, because joining the chorus means belonging to him forever. In the end Mara sings the verse alone, unbinding the chorus at the cost of her own documented existence — she survives, but no photograph, record, or memory of anyone but Jonah now contains her.
about_author: Paloma Oyelaran is a Lagos-born, Manchester-based writer whose horror draws on oral tradition, family archives, and the things photographs refuse to show. She spent six years documenting abandoned infrastructure before turning her field notes into fiction.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. While mapping storm drains for her documentation blog, Mara notices a junction that contradicts every municipal survey — a corridor that measures longer inside than outside. She photographs it obsessively; the photos come back slightly wrong, shadows leaning toward the camera. Emotional beat: thrill curdling into unease.

chapters.title: Everything Is a Prayer
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Flashback-woven chapter establishing why Mara documents everything: after their mother vanished when they were children, only her notebooks proved she existed. Jonah teases her about it; grandma Rosa warns her that some things get stronger when you write them down. Emotional beat: tenderness and foreshadowing.

chapters.title: Grandma's Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Sorting boxes at Grandma Rosa's house, Mara scans forty years of family photographs and finds the same anomaly in all of them: a plain wooden chair against the far wall, empty, present even in pictures taken decades apart. No one in the family remembers owning it. Emotional beat: quiet dread taking root.

chapters.title: Jonah Goes Down
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Worried about his sister's obsession, Jonah follows her map into the tunnels alone to prove there's nothing there. He hears humming — many voices, one melody — and films it. His last phone video shows him turning toward something off-screen and smiling in a way that isn't his. Emotional beat: bravado collapsing into terror.

chapters.title: The Photograph Moves
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. A photo of the family kitchen, timestamped yesterday, now shows Jonah seated in the extra chair, eyes closed, mouth open mid-song. Rosa burns the print; it reappears intact inside Mara's camera bag. Emotional beat: grief arriving before loss is confirmed.

chapters.title: Descent Protocol
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara prepares like an expedition: rope, air meters, printed backups of everything, a dead-man switch email. She leaves instructions with her friend Dev, the only person she tells. Rosa refuses to explain what she knows, only pressing an old hymnal into Mara's hands. Emotional beat: resolve built on fear.

chapters.title: The Chorus Below
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. In the tunnels, the humming resolves into words — a lullaby in a language Rosa sang once and never again. Dozens of figures stand in alcoves, singing with eyes shut, including people from missing-person posters Mara has photographed over the years. None of them will look at her. Emotional beat: horror of recognition.

chapters.title: The Smiling Man
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She sees him at the end of the corridor: tall, seated on a chair identical to the one in the photographs, smiling without moving his face. He speaks without sound, and she understands anyway — he knows her name, her mother's name, and offers to tell her where her mother went if she takes a seat. Emotional beat: temptation wearing a friendly mask.

chapters.title: Rules of the House
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Fleeing deeper, Mara meets Odile, a woman who has survived in the tunnels for thirty years by never singing, never sleeping in the same alcove twice, and never answering when the chorus uses her voice. Odile explains the Smiling Man feeds on belonging; the song binds singers to him. Emotional beat: desperate mentorship.

chapters.title: What Rosa Buried
chapters.summary: Rosa's POV. Interlude above ground: Rosa confronts the hymnal, revealing through memory that as a girl she sang the song's first three verses in a village church basement, and everyone who sang with her was slowly erased from the world while she alone escaped because she stopped mid-verse. She has been hiding from the fourth verse her whole life. Emotional beat: guilt finally surfacing.

chapters.title: Jonah, Singing
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara finds Jonah among the chorus, physically present but hollow-eyed, mouthing the verses perfectly. He briefly surfaces when she says their mother's nickname, whispering that the man shows each singer exactly what they most want to belong to. Emotional beat: hope and heartbreak entangled.

chapters.title: The Verse Nobody Wrote Down
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile reveals the truth she's guarded: there is a last verse, sung only by the Smiling Man himself, and hearing it fully is how he claims you. But a fragment survives — carried by the first person he ever took, kept alive somewhere in the deepest gallery. Odile has never dared go. Emotional beat: cowardice confessed, courage requested.

chapters.title: Dev Counts the Days
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Above ground, Dev waits out the dead-man switch deadline, digging through archives and finding that the tunnel network matches the footprint of a demolished orphanage where children disappeared in 1954 — and that Mara's mother's name appears on its intake ledger. Emotional beat: dread compounding into determination.

chapters.title: The First Taken
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Guided by Odile's chalk marks, Mara reaches the deepest gallery and finds the first victim: a man preserved mid-sentence since 1954, still whispering the last verse's opening lines on loop. To learn it she must sit close enough for him to see her — and the Smiling Man begins walking down the corridor toward them. Emotional beat: race against inevitability.

chapters.title: Learning Without Singing
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara memorizes the verse silently, mouthing nothing, while the first victim's whisper frays and the Smiling Man's smile widens with each line she absorbs. He offers her mother one final time; Mara realizes her mother chose this trade decades ago to keep Rosa safe. Emotional beat: fury replacing fear.

chapters.title: The Chorus Turns
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The Smiling Man commands the chorus to sing the claiming verse at Mara directly. Jonah breaks formation to shield her, buying seconds, his borrowed smile cracking. Odile arrives and sacrifices her thirty years of silence, singing loudly to draw the man's attention. Emotional beat: loyalty weaponized against power.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Alone before the chair, Mara sings the final verse aloud — the only way to end it is to complete it, alone, giving the song nowhere else to bind. The chorus collapses mid-note; the Smiling Man's smile finally moves, becoming something like relief, then nothing. The tunnels begin folding shut around her. Emotional beat: terrible triumph.

chapters.title: Running Out of Song
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara drags Jonah toward the surface as the corridors erase themselves behind them, passing the first victim finally at rest and Odile's chalk marks fading to blank stone. She realizes the song is taking payment as they climb: every memory of her is being unwritten. Emotional beat: sacrifice understood too late to stop.

chapters.title: The Empty Frame
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Above ground, Jonah wakes in a hospital, rescued but unable to say by whom. Every photograph of the two siblings now shows him alone; Dev remembers a sister-shaped absence; Rosa weeps at a granddaughter she can't name. Only Jonah, marked by the tunnels, still sees Mara standing in the room. Emotional beat: grief and gratitude fused.

chapters.title: Documentation
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Unrecorded by any camera or database, Mara rebuilds proof of herself the old way: handwriting, spoken testimony, Jonah's memory as her only archive. She and Rosa finally speak plainly about the village, the church basement, and Mara's mother's choice. Emotional beat: reconciliation through shared truth.

chapters.title: The Chair Comes Back
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Months later, a new family photograph develops with a faint second shadow beside Jonah — not the Smiling Man, but something gentler. Jonah chooses to leave it in the frame rather than burn it, telling no one. Emotional beat: ambiguous peace, love outlasting erasure.

chapters.title: Verse One, Again
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Closing chapter: Mara returns to the sealed tunnel entrance at dawn and hums the first three verses softly — not to call anything, but to prove she can carry the song without being owned by it. Somewhere below, faintly, something hums back a note she taught it. She walks away, undocumented and free. Emotional beat: hard-won autonomy, door left deliberately ajar.
